t1.title: System architecture design
t1.prompt: Design a system connection architecture for a web app with Node.js backend, SQL database (assume PostgreSQL), and React frontend. The app manages a mechanical devices inventory (fields like name, reference, quantity, etc). There are three roles: user (read all records, update individual records), staff (also add new records, submit bulk updates), and admin (also create/delete database fields dynamically and manage users). Describe: overall architecture diagram (components: React SPA, REST/GraphQL API, Node.js/Express backend, SQL database, auth service), authentication/authorization flow (JWT-based with role-based access control), how dynamic DB field creation by admin would be handled safely (e.g. schema migration strategy or EAV pattern), request flow for bulk updates, and security best practices (input validation, rate limiting, HTTPS, password hashing, RBAC middleware, audit logging). Present as clear structured text with headers.
t1.criteria: Provides a clear, structured architecture description covering components, data flow, auth/RBAC, dynamic schema handling, and security best practices.
t1.result:
# System Connection Architecture — Mechanical Devices Inventory

## 1. Overall Architecture

### 1.1 Component Diagram (text form)

```
                         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                         │        Client (Browser)      │
                         │  React SPA (Vite/CRA)        │
                         │  - React Router              │
                         │  - TanStack Query / RTK Query│
                         │  - Auth context (in-memory   │
                         │    access token)             │
                         └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                                         │ HTTPS only (TLS 1.2+)
                                         │ JSON over REST
                                         ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                         │   CDN / Static Host          │
                         │  (serves built SPA assets)   │
                         └──────────────────────────────┘
                                         │
                                         ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                         │  Reverse Proxy / API Gateway │
                         │  Nginx or Traefik            │
                         │  - TLS termination           │
                         │  - HSTS, security headers    │
                         │  - Global rate limiting      │
                         │  - Request size limits       │
                         └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                                         │ HTTP (private network)
                                         ▼
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │            Node.js / Express API (stateless, N replicas)       │
      │                                                                │
      │  Middleware chain:                                             │
      │   helmet → cors → body parser → rate limiter →                 │
      │   requestId/logger → authenticate(JWT) → authorize(role) →     │
      │   validate(schema) → controller → error handler                │
      │                                                                │
      │  Modules:                                                      │
      │   • auth/          (login, refresh, logout, password reset)    │
      │   • users/         (admin-only user management)                │
      │   • devices/       (CRUD, list, search, individual update)     │
      │   • bulk/          (bulk update job submission + status)       │
      │   • schema/        (admin dynamic field create/delete)         │
      │   • audit/         (audit log write + query)                   │
      └───────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────┬─────────────────┘
              │                  │                   │
              ▼                  ▼                   ▼
  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   PostgreSQL      │  │  Redis         │  │  Worker Process      │
  │  - devices        │  │ - refresh token│  │ (BullMQ consumer)    │
  │  - device_values  │  │   allow/deny   │  │ - bulk update jobs   │
  │  - field_defs     │  │ - rate limits  │  │ - CSV parsing        │
  │  - users          │  │ - job queue    │  │ - schema migrations  │
  │  - audit_log      │  │ - cache        │  │   (serialized)       │
  │  - bulk_jobs      │  └────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────┘
              │
              ▼
  ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Object storage    │
  │ (S3/MinIO):       │
  │ bulk CSV uploads, │
  │ job result files  │
  └───────────────────┘
```

### 1.2 Component Responsibilities

| Component | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **React SPA** | UI, client-side routing, optimistic reads, role-driven UI gating (cosmetic only — never the security boundary). Renders dynamic columns from a `/schema/fields` descriptor. |
| **Reverse proxy** | TLS termination, HSTS, compression, coarse rate limiting, blocking oversized bodies before they reach Node. |
| **Express API** | The single authoritative enforcement point for authN/authZ, validation, business rules, and audit writes. Stateless → horizontally scalable. |
| **Auth service** | Logically separate module (can be extracted into its own service or replaced by Keycloak/Auth0 later). Issues and verifies JWTs, manages password hashes and refresh-token rotation. |
| **PostgreSQL** | System of record. Holds inventory, user accounts, field metadata, audit trail, bulk-job state. |
| **Redis** | Refresh-token/session denylist, distributed rate-limit counters, BullMQ queue backend, short-TTL cache of the field-definition schema. |
| **Worker** | Executes long-running bulk updates and DDL migrations off the request path so HTTP stays fast and DDL is serialized. |

### 1.3 API Style Choice

**Recommendation: REST** for this application.

- The domain is a small set of well-bounded resources (`/devices`, `/users`, `/schema/fields`, `/bulk-jobs`).
- Bulk/async operations map cleanly onto `POST /bulk-jobs` + `GET /bulk-jobs/:id` (job-resource pattern), which is awkward in GraphQL.
- Per-field authorization and per-endpoint rate limiting are trivial in REST middleware; in GraphQL they require field-level resolver guards and query-cost analysis.
- Dynamic fields fight GraphQL's static typed schema (you'd end up with a `JSON` scalar anyway, losing GraphQL's main benefit).

Representative endpoints:

```
POST   /api/v1/auth/login                 public
POST   /api/v1/auth/refresh               public (cookie-bound)
POST   /api/v1/auth/logout                any authenticated

GET    /api/v1/devices                    user+   (paginated, filter, sort)
GET    /api/v1/devices/:id                user+
PATCH  /api/v1/devices/:id                user+   (single record update)
POST   /api/v1/devices                    staff+
DELETE /api/v1/devices/:id                staff+

POST   /api/v1/bulk-jobs                  staff+  (multipart CSV or JSON array)
GET    /api/v1/bulk-jobs/:id              staff+  (status/progress/errors)

GET    /api/v1/schema/fields              user+   (drives dynamic UI)
POST   /api/v1/schema/fields              admin
PATCH  /api/v1/schema/fields/:key         admin
DELETE /api/v1/schema/fields/:key         admin

GET    /api/v1/users                      admin
POST   /api/v1/users                      admin
PATCH  /api/v1/users/:id                  admin
DELETE /api/v1/users/:id                  admin

GET    /api/v1/audit-log                  admin
```

---

## 2. Authentication & Authorization Flow

### 2.1 Token Strategy

| Token | Lifetime | Storage | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Access JWT** | 15 min | React memory (never `localStorage`) | `sub`, `role`, `tokenVersion`, `iat`, `exp`, `iss`, `aud`, `jti` |
| **Refresh token** | 7–30 days, rotating | `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie scoped to `/api/v1/auth` | Opaque random 256-bit value, hashed in DB/Redis |

Access tokens are signed with **RS256** (asymmetric) so any future microservice can verify with the public key without holding the signing secret. Keep a `kid` header to allow key rotation.

Keep the JWT payload minimal — only `role`, never permission lists, so that role changes don't require re-issuing large tokens.

### 2.2 Login Flow

```
React                Express /auth/login           PostgreSQL         Redis
  │                          │                          │               │
  │ POST {email, password}   │                          │               │
  ├─────────────────────────►│                          │               │
  │                          │ rate-limit check (IP+email)──────────────►│
  │                          │ SELECT user by email     │               │
  │                          ├─────────────────────────►│               │
  │                          │◄─────────────────────────┤               │
  │                          │ argon2.verify(hash, pw)  │               │
  │                          │   (constant-time; run    │               │
  │                          │   dummy hash if user     │               │
  │                          │   not found)             │               │
  │                          │ sign access JWT (15m)    │               │
  │                          │ generate refresh token,  │               │
  │                          │ store SHA-256 hash ──────────────────────►│
  │                          │ INSERT audit_log(LOGIN)  │               │
  │                          ├─────────────────────────►│               │
  │ 200 {accessToken, user}  │                          │               │
  │ Set-Cookie: rt=...       │                          │               │
  │◄─────────────────────────┤                          │               │
```

Failed logins return a generic `401 Invalid credentials` (no user-enumeration signal) and increment a counter; after N failures the account is temporarily locked.

### 2.3 Authenticated Request Flow

```
1. React attaches  Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
2. authenticate middleware:
     - extract + verify signature, iss, aud, exp
     - reject if jti in Redis denylist (logout / forced revoke)
     - compare token.tokenVersion with cached user.tokenVersion
       → mismatch means role changed or admin revoked ⇒ 401
     - attach req.user = { id, role, tokenVersion }
3. authorize('staff') middleware:
     - ROLE_RANK = { user: 1, staff: 2, admin: 3 }
     - if ROLE_RANK[req.user.role] < ROLE_RANK[required] ⇒ 403
4. validate(schema) middleware (Zod/Joi) on params, query, body
5. Controller → service → repository (parameterized SQL)
6. Audit middleware records mutating operations
```

### 2.4 Silent Refresh

On `401 token_expired`, an Axios/fetch response interceptor calls `POST /auth/refresh` (cookie sent automatically), receives a new access token, and replays the original request once. Concurrent 401s are coalesced into a single in-flight refresh promise to avoid a refresh stampede.

**Refresh rotation with reuse detection:** every refresh invalidates the old token and issues a new one. If an already-used refresh token is presented, the entire token family for that user is revoked (bump `tokenVersion`) and a `SECURITY_TOKEN_REUSE` audit event is logged — this defeats replay of a stolen refresh cookie.

### 2.5 Role Capability Matrix

| Capability | user | staff | admin |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Read all device records | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Update an individual record | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create a new record | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Delete a record | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Submit bulk update | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create / delete dynamic fields | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Manage users & roles | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Read audit log | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

Enforced centrally by a declarative permission map rather than scattered `if` statements:

```js
// permissions.js
const PERMISSIONS = {
  'device:read':    ['user', 'staff', 'admin'],
  'device:update':  ['user', 'staff', 'admin'],
  'device:create':  ['staff', 'admin'],
  'device:delete':  ['staff', 'admin'],
  'bulk:submit':    ['staff', 'admin'],
  'schema:manage':  ['admin'],
  'user:manage':    ['admin'],
  'audit:read':     ['admin'],
};

const can = (perm) => (req, res, next) =>
  PERMISSIONS[perm]?.includes(req.user.role)
    ? next()
    : res.status(403).json({ error: 'forbidden', required: perm });

// usage
router.post('/devices', authenticate, can('device:create'), validate(createDeviceSchema), ctrl.create);
```

**Field-level authorization:** the `field_definitions` table carries `min_role_read` and `min_role_write`. A serializer strips fields the caller may not read, and the update validator rejects writes to fields above the caller's role — so a `user` can update `quantity` and `location` but not, say, `unit_cost`, without needing separate endpoints.

---

## 3. Dynamic Field Creation by Admin

### 3.1 Recommendation: Hybrid — fixed core columns + JSONB for dynamic attributes, governed by a metadata table

Pure EAV (`entity_attribute_value`) is rejected: every query becomes a pile of self-joins, type safety is lost, and reporting performance collapses. Uncontrolled runtime `ALTER TABLE` is also rejected: it grants the app role DDL rights, risks table locks under load, and drifts from version-controlled migrations.

The hybrid gives typed, indexed core fields plus safe, unlimited extensibility.

### 3.2 Schema

```sql
-- Core, stable columns: known at build time, in real migrations
CREATE TABLE devices (
  id          BIGGENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  reference   TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  quantity    INTEGER     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (quantity >= 0),
  location    TEXT,
  status      TEXT        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  attributes  JSONB       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,   -- dynamic fields live here
  version     INTEGER     NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,             -- optimistic locking
  created_by  BIGINT      REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ                                  -- soft delete
);

CREATE INDEX idx_devices_attributes ON devices USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_name_trgm  ON devices USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);

-- The metadata registry: the contract between admin, API, and UI
CREATE TABLE field_definitions (
  id              BIGGENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  key             TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE          -- ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$
                    CHECK (key ~ '^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$'),
  label           TEXT    NOT NULL,
  data_type       TEXT    NOT NULL
                    CHECK (data_type IN ('string','integer','decimal','boolean','date','enum','text')),
  enum_values     JSONB,                            -- required iff data_type='enum'
  is_required     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  default_value   JSONB,
  validation      JSONB,                            -- {min,max,maxLength,pattern}
  storage         TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'jsonb'  -- 'jsonb' | 'column'
                    CHECK (storage IN ('jsonb','column')),
  is_indexed      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  min_role_read   TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user',
  min_role_write  TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user',
  display_order   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  status          TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' -- active | deprecated | archived
                    CHECK (status IN ('active','deprecated','archived')),
  created_by      BIGINT  REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  archived_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
```

### 3.3 Field Creation Flow

```
Admin (React)
   │  POST /api/v1/schema/fields
   │  { key:"torque_nm", label:"Torque (Nm)", data_type:"decimal",
   │    is_required:false, validation:{min:0,max:10000}, is_indexed:true }
   ▼
authenticate → can('schema:manage') → validate(fieldDefSchema)
   ▼
Service layer:
  1. Normalize key to snake_case; assert regex ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$
  2. Assert key ∉ RESERVED  (id, name, reference, quantity, location,
                             status, version, created_at, updated_at,
                             deleted_at, attributes, select, from, where, ...)
  3. Assert key not already present (active OR archived) — no silent reuse
  4. Assert count(active fields) < MAX_DYNAMIC_FIELDS (e.g. 200)
  5. Acquire pg_advisory_xact_lock(SCHEMA_LOCK_ID)  ← serializes all DDL/meta changes
  6. BEGIN
       INSERT INTO field_definitions (...)
       IF is_indexed:
          enqueue CREATE_INDEX job (worker runs it CONCURRENTLY, outside txn)
       INSERT INTO audit_log (action='FIELD_CREATE', ...)
     COMMIT
  7. Invalidate Redis key `schema:fields`; bump schemaVersion
   ▼
201 Created → React refetches GET /schema/fields → forms & tables re-render
```

**The critical safety property: no identifier ever reaches SQL from user input.** The admin's `key` is stored as *data* inside a JSONB document, never concatenated into a query. Reads use parameterized JSONB paths:

```js
// SAFE — key travels as a bound parameter, not as SQL text
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `SELECT id, name, reference, quantity, attributes
     FROM devices
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
      AND attributes @> jsonb_build_object($1::text, $2::text)
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT $3 OFFSET $4`,
  [fieldKey, fieldValue, limit, offset]
);
```

The only place an identifier is interpolated is the optional expression index, and only after the key has passed the strict regex whitelist **and** been re-validated against the persisted `field_definitions` row (never against raw request input):

```js
// Worker, background, after whitelist validation against stored metadata
const def = await getFieldDefinitionFromDb(key);          // source of truth
assert(/^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$/.test(def.key));            // belt and braces
const idx = `idx_devices_attr_${def.key}`;
await pool.query(
  `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS ${pgFormat.ident(idx)}
     ON devices (((attributes ->> ${pgFormat.literal(def.key)})))`
);
```

`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids the long write lock that would otherwise stall the inventory table.

### 3.4 Field Deletion Flow — Soft, Staged, Reversible

Hard-deleting data on an admin click is unacceptable for an inventory system. Deletion is a three-stage lifecycle:

| Stage | Action | Data | Reversible |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Deprecate** | `PATCH /schema/fields/:key {status:'deprecated'}` | Intact | ✅ instantly |
| **2. Archive** | `DELETE /schema/fields/:key` | Intact in JSONB, hidden from all API responses and UI | ✅ by admin |
| **3. Purge** | Scheduled job, only after retention window (e.g. 90 days) + explicit second confirmation | `attributes = attributes - 'key'` in batches; snapshot exported to object storage first | ❌ |

```
DELETE /api/v1/schema/fields/torque_nm
   ▼
authenticate → can('schema:manage') → require header X-Confirm-Field-Key: torque_nm
   ▼
  UPDATE field_definitions
     SET status='archived', archived_at=now()
   WHERE key=$1;
  DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_devices_attr_torque_nm;   -- whitelisted ident
  INSERT INTO audit_log (action='FIELD_ARCHIVE', actor, before_state, ...);
   ▼
200 { status:'archived', purgeEligibleAt:'2025-08-01T00:00:00Z' }
```

The purge itself runs batched (`... WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2` in 5 000-row chunks) so it never holds a long transaction against the live table.

### 3.5 When to Promote a JSONB Field to a Real Column

If a dynamic field becomes hot (heavy filtering/sorting/aggregation), an admin can promote it. This is handled as a **generated, reviewable migration file**, not a live DDL button:

1. Admin clicks "Promote to column" → system **generates** a migration script and opens it for review; it does **not** execute immediately in production.
2. The worker (or CI deploy) runs, in order:
   `ALTER TABLE devices ADD COLUMN torque_nm NUMERIC;` (instant — nullable, no default rewrite)
   backfill in batches from `attributes->>'torque_nm'`
   `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`
   flip `field_definitions.storage = 'column'`
   drop the key from `attributes` in batches
3. The repository layer reads `storage` from metadata and transparently routes reads/writes to either the column or the JSONB path, so application code and the React client are unaffected.

This keeps schema evolution inside version-controlled migrations (node-pg-migrate / Umzug / Prisma Migrate) while still giving admins self-service.

### 3.6 Database Privilege Separation

```
app_rw    → SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on data tables.  NO DDL.  ← API runtime uses this
migrator  → DDL rights (CREATE/ALTER/DROP/INDEX).                    ← worker + CI only
app_ro    → SELECT only.                                             ← reporting/read replica
```

Even a successful SQL injection against the API cannot alter the schema, because the runtime role has no DDL grant.

### 3.7 Validation Driven by Metadata

Field definitions are compiled into a runtime validator, cached in Redis and invalidated on any schema change:

t2.title: Helper libraries list
t2.prompt: Provide a specific list of recommended helper code libraries/packages for building a scalable, secure Node.js + SQL (PostgreSQL) + React web app with role-based access control (user, staff, admin roles) for a mechanical devices inventory system. Include categories: backend framework (e.g. Express), ORM/query builder (e.g. Sequelize or Knex), authentication (e.g. jsonwebtoken, bcrypt), validation (e.g. Joi or express-validator), security middleware (e.g. helmet, cors, express-rate-limit), logging (e.g. winston or pino), testing (e.g. Jest, Supertest), frontend (React Router, Redux/Zustand or React Query, Axios, Formik/Yup, Material UI or similar), and dev tools (ESLint, Prettier, Husky, dotenv). For each library, give a one-line justification.
t2.criteria: A categorized list of specific, real npm packages with brief justification for each, covering backend, frontend, security, and dev tooling.
t2.result:
# Recommended Libraries for Node.js + PostgreSQL + React RBAC Inventory App

## Backend Framework
- **express** — minimal, mature, huge ecosystem for REST APIs
- **express-async-errors** — cleanly handle async route errors without try/catch boilerplate

## ORM / Query Builder
- **Sequelize** — full-featured ORM with migrations, associations, and PostgreSQL support; good fit for structured inventory schemas with roles/relations
- (Alt: **Knex** + **Objection.js** if you want lighter query building with optional ORM layer)

## Authentication & Authorization
- **jsonwebtoken** — issue/verify JWTs for stateless session auth
- **bcrypt** — secure password hashing with salting
- **passport** + **passport-jwt** — standardized auth middleware strategy if you need pluggable auth (OAuth later)
- **express-rbac** or custom middleware using **casl** — declarative role/permission checks (user/staff/admin)

## Validation
- **Joi** — schema-based validation for request bodies, clear and reusable schemas
- **express-validator** — alternative, integrates directly into route middleware chain

## Security Middleware
- **helmet** — sets secure HTTP headers by default
- **cors** — controlled cross-origin access configuration
- **express-rate-limit** — throttle requests to prevent brute-force/DoS
- **express-mongo-sanitize**-equivalent not needed for SQL, but use **pg** parameterized queries/ORM to prevent injection
- **hpp** — protect against HTTP parameter pollution

## Logging
- **winston** — flexible, multi-transport logging (files, console, external services)
- **morgan** — HTTP request logging middleware, pairs well with winston

## Testing
- **Jest** — test runner + assertions, widely supported
- **Supertest** — HTTP assertions for testing Express routes end-to-end
- **sinon** — mocking/stubbing for isolating unit tests

## Frontend (React)
- **react-router-dom** — client-side routing including role-protected routes
- **@tanstack/react-query** — server-state caching/fetching, reduces boilerplate vs Redux for API data
- **Zustand** — lightweight global state for UI/auth state (simpler than Redux)
- **axios** — HTTP client with interceptors for attaching JWTs and handling errors
- **Formik** + **Yup** — form state management and schema validation matching backend rules
- **Material UI (MUI)** — accessible, themeable component library speeding up UI development

## Dev Tools
- **ESLint** — enforce code quality/consistency
- **Prettier** — automatic code formatting
- **Husky** + **lint-staged** — pre-commit hooks to run lint/tests before commits
- **dotenv** — manage environment variables/secrets across environments
- **nodemon** — auto-restart server during development
t2.notes:
- Chose Sequelize as primary ORM recommendation (alt: Knex/Objection) — later tasks should pick one, not mix.
- RBAC suggested via custom middleware or CASL library; no single canonical "express-rbac" is industry-standard — implementation detail is open for backend task to decide.
- Zustand recommended over Redux for simplicity; React Query handles server state separately — clarify this split in frontend architecture task.
- Security stack assumes PostgreSQL via parameterized queries/ORM (no injection-specific sanitizer library needed, unlike MongoDB).
- Testing stack assumes Jest as unified runner for both unit and integration (via Supertest) — frontend testing (React Testing Library) not included here, should be added by frontend task if needed.

# Ticket 1: Project Scaffolding, Repository Setup & CI/CD Pipeline

## Description / Goal
Establish the foundational project structure for the Mechanical Devices Inventory web app, including repository layout, backend (Node.js) and frontend (React) initialization, environment configuration, code quality tooling, containerization, and an automated CI/CD pipeline. This ticket sets the technical groundwork that all future feature development will build upon.

## Tasks / Acceptance Criteria

- **Repository Structure**
  - Set up a monorepo (e.g., using npm workspaces or Turborepo) with `/apps/api` (Node.js/Express backend) and `/apps/web` (React frontend) directories, plus a shared `/packages` folder for common types/utils.
  - Add a root-level `README.md` describing project structure, setup instructions, and scripts.

- **Backend Initialization**
  - Scaffold Node.js/Express (or NestJS) API with basic health-check endpoint (`GET /health`).

# Ticket 4: Core Inventory API, Bulk Updates & Dynamic Field Management

## Short Description / Goal
Implement the core backend API for managing mechanical device inventory records, including standard CRUD operations, a transaction-safe bulk update endpoint, and full support for dynamic custom fields/attributes. Enforce role-based permissions (User, Staff, Admin) and ensure all inputs are validated with a schema library (Zod/Joi). Cover functionality with automated integration tests.

## Tasks / Acceptance Criteria

- **Device CRUD Endpoints**
  - `GET /devices` — list devices with pagination (`page`, `limit`), filtering (by name, reference, custom field values), and sorting (by any core or dynamic field). Accessible to User, Staff, Admin.
  - `GET /devices/:id` — retrieve single device with all core + dynamic field values.
  - `POST /devices` — create new device (Staff/Admin only), validated against schema requiring `name`, `reference`, `quantity`, and optional dynamic field values matching defined field types.
  - `PUT /devices/:id` — update individual device (User, Staff, Admin), validated payload; Users restricted to updating only allowed fields (no dynamic field schema changes).
  - `DELETE /devices/:id` — remove device (Staff/Admin only).

- **Bulk Update Endpoint**
  - `PATCH /devices/bulk` (Staff/Admin only) accepts an array of `{id, fields}` updates.
  - Wrap all updates in a single DB transaction — if any single record update fails validation or DB constraint, roll back the entire batch and return detailed per-record error report.
  - Return summary response: count updated, list of failures with reasons.

- **Dynamic Field Definition Management (Admin only)**
  - `GET /field-definitions` — list all custom field definitions (name, type, required flag, options if enum).
  - `POST /field-definitions` — create new dynamic field (validate unique name, allowed types: string, number, boolean, date, enum).
  - `DELETE /field-definitions/:id` — delete a dynamic field definition and cascade-remove associated stored values from all devices.
  - Prevent deletion or type-change of a field definition if it would break existing device data integrity without explicit confirmation flag.

- **Schema/Payload Validation**
  - Implement Zod or Joi schemas for: device creation/update, bulk update payload, field definition creation.
  - Dynamic field values in device payloads must be validated against the current field definition types/constraints at runtime (not just static schema).
  - Return standardized 400 error responses with field-level validation messages.

- **Permissions Enforcement**
  - Add middleware checks per route matching the role matrix (User/Staff/Admin) as defined in project context.
  - Return 403 for unauthorized role attempts.

- **Automated Integration Tests**
  - Test CRUD endpoints for success and permission-denied cases per role.
  - Test bulk update transaction rollback behavior on partial failure.
  - Test dynamic field creation, validation enforcement on device payloads, and cascade deletion behavior.
  - Test pagination/filtering/sorting query correctness with seeded data.
t3.t1.t4.notes:
- Assumes DB schema already supports a dynamic key/value or EAV-style table for custom fields (from earlier ticket) — verify this exists before implementation.
- Role-based middleware (User/Staff/Admin) must already be established from auth ticket; this ticket only applies it to new routes.
- Bulk update must use DB transactions (e.g., pg `BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK` or ORM transaction wrapper) — critical for data integrity.
- Field definition deletion cascades to device data — needs explicit confirmation flag to avoid accidental data loss.
- Dynamic field validation must be enforced at runtime against current field definitions, not just static request schema.

# Recommended Libraries for Node.js + PostgreSQL + React RBAC Inventory App

## Backend Framework
- **express** — minimal, mature, huge ecosystem for REST APIs
- **express-async-errors** — cleanly handle async route errors without try/catch boilerplate

## ORM / Query Builder
- **Sequelize** — full-featured ORM with migrations, associations, and PostgreSQL support; good fit for structured inventory schemas with roles/relations
- (Alt: **Knex** + **Objection.js** if you want lighter query building with optional ORM layer)

## Authentication & Authorization
- **jsonwebtoken** — issue/verify JWTs for stateless session auth
- **bcrypt** — secure password hashing with salting
- **passport** + **passport-jwt** — standardized auth middleware strategy if you need pluggable auth (OAuth later)
- **express-rbac** or custom middleware using **casl** — declarative role/permission checks (user/staff/admin)

## Validation
- **Joi** — schema-based validation for request bodies, clear and reusable schemas
- **express-validator** — alternative, integrates directly into route middleware chain

## Security Middleware
- **helmet** — sets secure HTTP headers by default
- **cors** — controlled cross-origin access configuration
- **express-rate-limit** — throttle requests to prevent brute-force/DoS
- **express-mongo-sanitize**-equivalent not needed for SQL, but use **pg** parameterized queries/ORM to prevent injection
- **hpp** — protect against HTTP parameter pollution

## Logging
- **winston** — flexible, multi-transport logging (files, console, external services)
- **morgan** — HTTP request logging middleware, pairs well with winston

## Testing
- **Jest** — test runner + assertions, widely supported
- **Supertest** — HTTP assertions for testing Express routes end-to-end
- **sinon** — mocking/stubbing for isolating unit tests

## Frontend (React)
- **react-router-dom** — client-side routing including role-protected routes
- **@tanstack/react-query** — server-state caching/fetching, reduces boilerplate vs Redux for API data
- **Zustand** — lightweight global state for UI/auth state (simpler than Redux)
- **axios** — HTTP client with interceptors for attaching JWTs and handling errors
- **Formik** + **Yup** — form state management and schema validation matching backend rules
- **Material UI (MUI)** — accessible, themeable component library speeding up UI development

## Dev Tools
- **ESLint** — enforce code quality/consistency
- **Prettier** — automatic code formatting
- **Husky** + **lint-staged** — pre-commit hooks to run lint/tests before commits
- **dotenv** — manage environment variables/secrets across environments
- **nodemon** — auto-restart server during development
events.notes:
- Chose Sequelize as primary ORM recommendation (alt: Knex/Objection) — later tasks should pick one, not mix.
- RBAC suggested via custom middleware or CASL library; no single canonical "express-rbac" is industry-standard — implementation detail is open for backend task to decide.
- Zustand recommended over Redux for simplicity; React Query handles server state separately — clarify this split in frontend architecture task.
- Security stack assumes PostgreSQL via parameterized queries/ORM (no injection-specific sanitizer library needed, unlike MongoDB).
- Testing stack assumes Jest as unified runner for both unit and integration (via Supertest) — frontend testing (React Testing Library) not included here, should be added by frontend task if needed.

  - `POST /devices` — create new device (Staff/Admin only), validated against schema requiring `name`, `reference`, `quantity`, and optional dynamic field values matching defined field types.
  - `PUT /devices/:id` — update individual device (User, Staff, Admin), validated payload; Users restricted to updating only allowed fields (no dynamic field schema changes).
  - `DELETE /devices/:id` — remove device (Staff/Admin only).

- **Bulk Update Endpoint**
  - `PATCH /devices/bulk` (Staff/Admin only) accepts an array of `{id, fields}` updates.
  - Wrap all updates in a single DB transaction — if any single record update fails validation or DB constraint, roll back the entire batch and return detailed per-record error report.
  - Return summary response: count updated, list of failures with reasons.

- **Dynamic Field Definition Management (Admin only)**
  - `GET /field-definitions` — list all custom field definitions (name, type, required flag, options if enum).
  - `POST /field-definitions` — create new dynamic field (validate unique name, allowed types: string, number, boolean, date, enum).
  - `DELETE /field-definitions/:id` — delete a dynamic field definition and cascade-remove associated stored values from all devices.
  - Prevent deletion or type-change of a field definition if it would break existing device data integrity without explicit confirmation flag.

- **Schema/Payload Validation**
  - Implement Zod or Joi schemas for: device creation/update, bulk update payload, field definition creation.
  - Dynamic field values in device payloads must be validated against the current field definition types/constraints at runtime (not just static schema).
  - Return standardized 400 error responses with field-level validation messages.

- **Permissions Enforcement**
  - Add middleware checks per route matching the role matrix (User/Staff/Admin) as defined in project context.
  - Return 403 for unauthorized role attempts.

- **Automated Integration Tests**
  - Test CRUD endpoints for success and permission-denied cases per role.
  - Test bulk update transaction rollback behavior on partial failure.
  - Test dynamic field creation, validation enforcement on device payloads, and cascade deletion behavior.
  - Test pagination/filtering/sorting query correctness with seeded data.

## 2. Authentication & Authorization Flow

### 2.1 Token Strategy

| Token | Lifetime | Storage | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Access JWT** | 15 min | React memory (never `localStorage`) | `sub`, `role`, `tokenVersion`, `iat`, `exp`, `iss`, `aud`, `jti` |
| **Refresh token** | 7–30 days, rotating | `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie scoped to `/api/v1/auth` | Opaque random 256-bit value, hashed in DB/Redis |

Access tokens are signed with **RS256** (asymmetric) so any future microservice can verify with the public key without holding the signing secret. Keep a `kid` header to allow key rotation.

Keep the JWT payload minimal — only `role`, never permission lists, so that role changes don't require re-issuing large tokens.

### 2.2 Login Flow

```
React                Express /auth/login           PostgreSQL         Redis
  │                          │                          │               │
  │ POST {email, password}   │                          │               │
  ├─────────────────────────►│                          │               │
  │                          │ rate-limit check (IP+email)──────────────►│
  │                          │ SELECT user by email     │               │
  │                          ├─────────────────────────►│               │
  │                          │◄─────────────────────────┤               │
  │                          │ argon2.verify(hash, pw)  │               │
  │                          │   (constant-time; run    │               │
  │                          │   dummy hash if user     │               │
  │                          │   not found)             │               │
  │                          │ sign access JWT (15m)    │               │
  │                          │ generate refresh token,  │               │
  │                          │ store SHA-256 hash ──────────────────────►│
  │                          │ INSERT audit_log(LOGIN)  │               │
  │                          ├─────────────────────────►│               │
  │ 200 {accessToken, user}  │                          │               │
  │ Set-Cookie: rt=...       │                          │               │
  │◄─────────────────────────┤                          │               │
```

Failed logins return a generic `401 Invalid credentials` (no user-enumeration signal) and increment a counter; after N failures the account is temporarily locked.

### 2.3 Authenticated Request Flow

```
1. React attaches  Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
2. authenticate middleware:
     - extract + verify signature, iss, aud, exp
     - reject if jti in Redis denylist (logout / forced revoke)
     - compare token.tokenVersion with cached user.tokenVersion
       → mismatch means role changed or admin revoked ⇒ 401
     - attach req.user = { id, role, tokenVersion }
3. authorize('staff') middleware:
     - ROLE_RANK = { user: 1, staff: 2, admin: 3 }
     - if ROLE_RANK[req.user.role] < ROLE_RANK[required] ⇒ 403
4. validate(schema) middleware (Zod/Joi) on params, query, body
5. Controller → service → repository (parameterized SQL)
6. Audit middleware records mutating operations
```

### 2.4 Silent Refresh

On `401 token_expired`, an Axios/fetch response interceptor calls `POST /auth/refresh` (cookie sent automatically), receives a new access token, and replays the original request once. Concurrent 401s are coalesced into a single in-flight refresh promise to avoid a refresh stampede.

**Refresh rotation with reuse detection:** every refresh invalidates the old token and issues a new one. If an already-used refresh token is presented, the entire token family for that user is revoked (bump `tokenVersion`) and a `SECURITY_TOKEN_REUSE` audit event is logged — this defeats replay of a stolen refresh cookie.

### 2.5 Role Capability Matrix

| Capability | user | staff | admin |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Read all device records | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Update an individual record | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create a new record | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Delete a record | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Submit bulk update | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create / delete dynamic fields | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Manage users & roles | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Read audit log | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

Enforced centrally by a declarative permission map rather than scattered `if` statements:

```js
// permissions.js
const PERMISSIONS = {
  'device:read':    ['user', 'staff', 'admin'],
  'device:update':  ['user', 'staff', 'admin'],
  'device:create':  ['staff', 'admin'],
  'device:delete':  ['staff', 'admin'],
  'bulk:submit':    ['staff', 'admin'],
  'schema:manage':  ['admin'],
  'user:manage':    ['admin'],
  'audit:read':     ['admin'],
};

const can = (perm) => (req, res, next) =>
  PERMISSIONS[perm]?.includes(req.user.role)
    ? next()
    : res.status(403).json({ error: 'forbidden', required: perm });

// usage
router.post('/devices', authenticate, can('device:create'), validate(createDeviceSchema), ctrl.create);
```

**Field-level authorization:** the `field_definitions` table carries `min_role_read` and `min_role_write`. A serializer strips fields the caller may not read, and the update validator rejects writes to fields above the caller's role — so a `user` can update `quantity` and `location` but not, say, `unit_cost`, without needing separate endpoints.

---

## 3. Dynamic Field Creation by Admin

### 3.1 Recommendation: Hybrid — fixed core columns + JSONB for dynamic attributes, governed by a metadata table

Pure EAV (`entity_attribute_value`) is rejected: every query becomes a pile of self-joins, type safety is lost, and reporting performance collapses. Uncontrolled runtime `ALTER TABLE` is also rejected: it grants the app role DDL rights, risks table locks under load, and drifts from version-controlled migrations.

The hybrid gives typed, indexed core fields plus safe, unlimited extensibility.

### 3.2 Schema

```sql
-- Core, stable columns: known at build time, in real migrations
CREATE TABLE devices (
  id          BIGGENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  reference   TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  quantity    INTEGER     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (quantity >= 0),
  location    TEXT,
  status      TEXT        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  attributes  JSONB       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,   -- dynamic fields live here
  version     INTEGER     NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,             -- optimistic locking
  created_by  BIGINT      REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ                                  -- soft delete
);

CREATE INDEX idx_devices_attributes ON devices USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_name_trgm  ON devices USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);

-- The metadata registry: the contract between admin, API, and UI
CREATE TABLE field_definitions (
  id              BIGGENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  key             TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE          -- ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$
                    CHECK (key ~ '^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$'),
  label           TEXT    NOT NULL,
  data_type       TEXT    NOT NULL
                    CHECK (data_type IN ('string','integer','decimal','boolean','date','enum','text')),
  enum_values     JSONB,                            -- required iff data_type='enum'
  is_required     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  default_value   JSONB,
  validation      JSONB,                            -- {min,max,maxLength,pattern}
  storage         TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'jsonb'  -- 'jsonb' | 'column'
                    CHECK (storage IN ('jsonb','column')),
  is_indexed      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  min_role_read   TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user',
  min_role_write  TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user',
  display_order   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  status          TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' -- active | deprecated | archived
                    CHECK (status IN ('active','deprecated','archived')),
  created_by      BIGINT  REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  archived_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
```

### 3.3 Field Creation Flow

```
Admin (React)
   │  POST /api/v1/schema/fields
   │  { key:"torque_nm", label:"Torque (Nm)", data_type:"decimal",
   │    is_required:false, validation:{min:0,max:10000}, is_indexed:true }
   ▼
authenticate → can('schema:manage') → validate(fieldDefSchema)
   ▼
Service layer:
  1. Normalize key to snake_case; assert regex ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$
  2. Assert key ∉ RESERVED  (id, name, reference, quantity, location,
                             status, version, created_at, updated_at,
                             deleted_at, attributes, select, from, where, ...)
  3. Assert key not already present (active OR archived) — no silent reuse
  4. Assert count(active fields) < MAX_DYNAMIC_FIELDS (e.g. 200)
  5. Acquire pg_advisory_xact_lock(SCHEMA_LOCK_ID)  ← serializes all DDL/meta changes
  6. BEGIN
       INSERT INTO field_definitions (...)
       IF is_indexed:
          enqueue CREATE_INDEX job (worker runs it CONCURRENTLY, outside txn)
       INSERT INTO audit_log (action='FIELD_CREATE', ...)
     COMMIT
  7. Invalidate Redis key `schema:fields`; bump schemaVersion
   ▼
201 Created → React refetches GET /schema/fields → forms & tables re-render
```

**The critical safety property: no identifier ever reaches SQL from user input.** The admin's `key` is stored as *data* inside a JSONB document, never concatenated into a query. Reads use parameterized JSONB paths:

```js
// SAFE — key travels as a bound parameter, not as SQL text
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `SELECT id, name, reference, quantity, attributes
     FROM devices
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
      AND attributes @> jsonb_build_object($1::text, $2::text)
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT $3 OFFSET $4`,
  [fieldKey, fieldValue, limit, offset]
);
```

The only place an identifier is interpolated is the optional expression index, and only after the key has passed the strict regex whitelist **and** been re-validated against the persisted `field_definitions` row (never against raw request input):

```js
// Worker, background, after whitelist validation against stored metadata
const def = await getFieldDefinitionFromDb(key);          // source of truth
assert(/^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,38}$/.test(def.key));            // belt and braces
const idx = `idx_devices_attr_${def.key}`;
await pool.query(
  `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS ${pgFormat.ident(idx)}
     ON devices (((attributes ->> ${pgFormat.literal(def.key)})))`
);
```

`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids the long write lock that would otherwise stall the inventory table.

### 3.4 Field Deletion Flow — Soft, Staged, Reversible

Hard-deleting data on an admin click is unacceptable for an inventory system. Deletion is a three-stage lifecycle:

| Stage | Action | Data | Reversible |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Deprecate** | `PATCH /schema/fields/:key {status:'deprecated'}` | Intact | ✅ instantly |
| **2. Archive** | `DELETE /schema/fields/:key` | Intact in JSONB, hidden from all API responses and UI | ✅ by admin |
| **3. Purge** | Scheduled job, only after retention window (e.g. 90 days) + explicit second confirmation | `attributes = attributes - 'key'` in batches; snapshot exported to object storage first | ❌ |

```
DELETE /api/v1/schema/fields/torque_nm
   ▼
authenticate → can('schema:manage') → require header X-Confirm-Field-Key: torque_nm
   ▼
  UPDATE field_definitions
     SET status='archived', archived_at=now()
   WHERE key=$1;
  DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_devices_attr_torque_nm;   -- whitelisted ident
  INSERT INTO audit_log (action='FIELD_ARCHIVE', actor, before_state, ...);
   ▼
200 { status:'archived', purgeEligibleAt:'2025-08-01T00:00:00Z' }
```

The purge itself runs batched (`... WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2` in 5 000-row chunks) so it never holds a long transaction against the live table.

### 3.5 When to Promote a JSONB Field to a Real Column

If a dynamic field becomes hot (heavy filtering/sorting/aggregation), an admin can promote it. This is handled as a **generated, reviewable migration file**, not a live DDL button:

1. Admin clicks "Promote to column" → system **generates** a migration script and opens it for review; it does **not** execute immediately in production.
2. The worker (or CI deploy) runs, in order:

# Mechanical Inventory Management System — Technical Proposal

## 1. System Architecture

### 1.1 High-Level Architecture

```
                                   ┌─────────────────────┐
                                   │      React SPA       │
                                   │  (Vite + TS + Query)  │
                                   └──────────┬───────────┘
                                              │ HTTPS/JWT
                                   ┌──────────▼───────────┐
                                   │   Nginx / Reverse     │
                                   │   Proxy + Rate Limit  │
                                   └──────────┬───────────┘
                                              │
                        ┌─────────────────────▼─────────────────────┐
                        │            Node.js / Express API           │
                        │  ┌────────────┬─────────────┬───────────┐ │
                        │  │ Controllers│  Services    │Middleware │ │
                        │  │ (routes)   │ (business    │(auth/rbac,│ │
                        │  │            │  logic)      │validation)│ │
                        │  └────────────┴─────────────┴───────────┘ │
                        └──────────┬───────────────────┬────────────┘
                                   │                    │
                   ┌───────────────▼───┐      ┌─────────▼─────────┐
                   │   PostgreSQL       │      │  Redis             │
                   │ (Prisma ORM)       │      │ (sessions, cache,  │
                   │ - users            │      │  rate-limit, queue)│
                   │ - inventory_items  │      └─────────┬─────────┘
                   │ - field_defs       │                │
                   │ - audit_logs       │      ┌─────────▼─────────┐
                   │ - bulk_jobs        │      │ BullMQ Worker      │
                   └────────────────────┘      │ (bulk upload proc, │
                                                │  async jobs)       │
                                                └────────────────────┘
                        ┌────────────────────┐
                        │  S3 / Local Storage │  (bulk CSV/XLSX files)
                        └────────────────────┘
```

### 1.2 Layered Backend Design

- **Routes** → **Controllers** (thin, HTTP-only) → **Services** (business logic) → **Repositories/Prisma** (data access)
- **Middleware pipeline**: `helmet` → `cors` → `rateLimiter` → `authenticate (JWT)` → `authorize (RBAC)` → `validate (schema)` → `controller`
- **Async processing**: bulk updates are uploaded, queued in Redis/BullMQ, processed by a worker, with job status polling endpoint (avoids blocking requests & timeouts).

### 1.3 Data Model Strategy (key decision)

To satisfy "admin can create/eliminate DB fields" **without unsafe runtime `ALTER TABLE`**, use a **hybrid fixed-column + metadata-driven dynamic field** pattern:

- Core inventory table has fixed, indexed columns: `name, reference, quantity, category, location`.
- A `field_definitions` table lets admins define **additional custom fields** (name, data type, validation rules, required flag).
- A `custom_fields JSONB` column on `inventory_items` stores values for those dynamic fields.
- Backend validates JSONB payloads against `field_definitions` dynamically (via Zod schema built at runtime).
- This avoids schema migrations at runtime, avoids table locks, keeps queries performant with GIN indexes on JSONB, and is the industry-accepted safe alternative to live schema changes.

### 1.4 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

| Action | User | Staff | Admin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read all inventory | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Update individual record | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create new record | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Bulk update (CSV/XLSX) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Create/delete custom fields | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Create/delete users | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

Implemented via a **permission matrix** (not hardcoded if-checks) loaded into middleware `authorize(resource, action)` — scalable if roles grow later.

**Tasks:**

### **Sprint 3 — Core Inventory Module (Read & Individual Update)**

**Tasks:**
1. Finalize `inventory_items` schema (fixed columns + `custom_fields JSONB`) and Prisma migration.

**Tasks:**

# Matrix Multiplication: Optimized Approach (Strassen's Algorithm)

## 1. The Baseline Problem

Standard matrix multiplication of two n×n matrices uses three nested loops:

```python
def naive_multiply(A, B, n):
    C = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            for k in range(n):
                C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]
    return C
```

**Complexity:** O(n³) multiplications. For n=1000, that's ~10⁹ operations — the bottleneck in ML, graphics, and scientific computing.

## 2. Strassen's Algorithm — Divide and Conquer

**Idea:** Split each n×n matrix into four (n/2)×(n/2) blocks:

```
A = [A11 A12]    B = [B11 B12]
    [A21 A22]        [B21 B22]
```

Naively, computing C = A·B this way still needs 8 block multiplications + 4 additions (no savings). Strassen's insight: combine blocks cleverly using only **7 multiplications** instead of 8, at the cost of extra additions (which are cheaper, O(n²)).

**The 7 products:**

```
M1 = (A11 + A22)(B11 + B22)
M2 = (A21 + A22) B11
M3 = A11 (B12 - B22)
M4 = A22 (B21 - B11)
M5 = (A11 + A12) B22
M6 = (A21 - A11)(B11 + B12)
M7 = (A12 - A22)(B21 + B22)
```

**Resulting blocks of C:**

```
C11 = M1 + M4 - M5 + M7
C12 = M3 + M5
C21 = M2 + M4
C22 = M1 - M2 + M3 + M6
```

```python
def strassen(A, B, n):
    if n == 1:
        return [[A[0][0] * B[0][0]]]
    
    mid = n // 2
    A11, A12, A21, A22 = split(A, mid)
    B11, B12, B21, B22 = split(B, mid)

    M1 = strassen(add(A11, A22), add(B11, B22), mid)
    M2 = strassen(add(A21, A22), B11, mid)
    M3 = strassen(A11, sub(B12, B22), mid)
    M4 = strassen(A22, sub(B21, B11), mid)
    M5 = strassen(add(A11, A12), B22, mid)
    M6 = strassen(sub(A21, A11), add(B11, B12), mid)
    M7 = strassen(sub(A12, A22), add(B21, B22), mid)

    C11 = add(sub(add(M1, M4), M5), M7)
    C12 = add(M3, M5)
    C21 = add(M2, M4)
    C22 = add(sub(add(M1, M3), M2), M6)

    return combine(C11, C12, C21, C22)
```

**Complexity:** Recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) → **O(n^log₂7) ≈ O(n^2.807)**.

## 3. What Can Be Improved (Critical Analysis)

**a) Constant overhead dominates at small sizes**

# Matrix Multiplication with Strassen's Algorithm

## The Naive Approach (Baseline)

Standard matrix multiplication for two n×n matrices uses three nested loops:

```python
def naive_multiply(A, B, n):
    C = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            for k in range(n):
                C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]
    return C
```

**Complexity:** O(n³) multiplications.

## Optimized Approach: Strassen's Algorithm

Strassen's insight: you can multiply two 2×2 matrices using **7 multiplications instead of 8** by cleverly combining additions/subtractions. Applied recursively to n×n matrices (split into quadrants), this reduces complexity to **O(n^2.807)**.

### Core Idea

For matrices split into quadrants:
```
A = [A11 A12]    B = [B11 B12]
    [A21 A22]        [B21 B22]
```

Compute 7 products (not 8):
```
M1 = (A11 + A22)(B11 + B22)
M2 = (A21 + A22)B11
M3 = A11(B12 - B22)
M4 = A22(B21 - B11)
M5 = (A11 + A12)B22
M6 = (A21 - A11)(B11 + B12)
M7 = (A12 - A22)(B21 + B22)
```

Then:
```
C11 = M1 + M4 - M5 + M7
C12 = M3 + M5
C21 = M2 + M4
C22 = M1 - M2 + M3 + M6
```

### Implementation

```python
import numpy as np

def strassen(A, B):
    n = A.shape[0]
    
    # Base case: small enough, use naive multiplication
    if n <= 64:  # threshold tuned for practical speed
        return A @ B
    
    mid = n // 2
    A11, A12 = A[:mid, :mid], A[:mid, mid:]
    A21, A22 = A[mid:, :mid], A[mid:, mid:]
    B11, B12 = B[:mid, :mid], B[:mid, mid:]
    B21, B22 = B[mid:, :mid], B[mid:, mid:]
    
    M1 = strassen(A11 + A22, B11 + B22)
    M2 = strassen(A21 + A22, B11)
    M3 = strassen(A11, B12 - B22)
    M4 = strassen(A22, B21 - B11)
    M5 = strassen(A11 + A12, B22)
    M6 = strassen(A21 - A11, B11 + B12)
    M7 = strassen(A12 - A22, B21 + B22)
    
    C11 = M1 + M4 - M5 + M7
    C12 = M3 + M5
    C21 = M2 + M4
    C22 = M1 - M2 + M3 + M6
    
    C = np.empty((n, n))
    C[:mid, :mid], C[:mid, mid:] = C11, C12
    C[mid:, :mid], C[mid:, mid:] = C21, C22
    return C
```

## Reasoning: What Can Be Improved

**1. Padding overhead for non-power-of-2 sizes**
Strassen's requires clean halving. Non-square or odd-dimension matrices need padding with zeros, wasting computation. A dynamic peeling strategy (handling odd rows/columns separately) reduces this waste.

**2. Numerical stability**
Strassen's involves more additions/subtractions than naive multiplication, which amplifies floating-point rounding errors — especially problematic for ill-conditioned matrices. Naive multiplication is more numerically stable. Mixing strategies (naive for small blocks, Strassen for large) mitigates this.

**3. Memory overhead**
The recursive splitting creates many temporary matrices (7 recursive calls × multiple additions each), increasing memory allocation and cache pressure. In-place computation or memory pooling can reduce allocation overhead.

**4. Threshold tuning**
The crossover point where Strassen's beats naive multiplication depends on hardware (cache size, memory bandwidth). A poorly tuned threshold hurts performance — this needs empirical calibration per system, or adaptive selection at runtime.

**5. Not the theoretical best**

siac.answer:
# Versioned SQL Schema Design

This is a classic hard problem in schema design. Here's a thorough approach covering the main strategies, trade-offs, and a concrete recommended pattern.

## The Core Problem

Versioning breaks naive foreign keys because:
- A "record" now has multiple physical rows (one per version)
- Other tables need to reference either a *specific version* or the *logical entity* (latest/any version)
- You need to preserve integrity for both historical queries (as-of-time) and current-state queries

## Key Design Decision: What Does a Foreign Key Point To?

You must decide, per relationship, whether references are to:

1. **The logical entity** (survives across versions) — most common, most useful
2. **A specific version** — needed for audit trails, snapshots, contracts referencing exact terms

Trying to make one mechanism serve both needs is where people get stuck. Design for both explicitly.

## Recommended Pattern: Surrogate Entity ID + Version Table

Separate the *stable identity* from the *versioned content*.

```sql
-- Stable identity, never changes, this is what everyone references
CREATE TABLE product (
    product_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    current_version_id BIGINT NULL  -- see below, chicken/egg handled via deferred FK
);

-- Every version of that entity's data
CREATE TABLE product_version (
    product_version_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES product(product_id),
    version_no          INT NOT NULL,

When you version a row, you get multiple physical rows representing "the same" logical entity over time. Foreign keys then face an ambiguity: does a reference point to:
- **A specific version** (immutable pointer, but breaks when you want "latest")
- **The logical entity** (stable pointer, but which version does it resolve to?)

Most naive designs break FK constraints or silently point to stale data. You need to pick an explicit strategy.

## Recommended Pattern: Surrogate Entity ID + Version Table

Separate the **identity** of an entity from its **versions**.

```sql
-- Identity table: one row per logical entity, immutable
CREATE TABLE entity (
    entity_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    entity_type TEXT NOT NULL, -- optional, if sharing an ID space
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Version table: one row per version, immutable once written
CREATE TABLE entity_version (
    version_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    entity_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES entity(entity_id),
    version_num INT NOT NULL,
    data JSONB NOT NULL, -- or real columns
    valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    valid_to TIMESTAMPTZ, -- NULL = current
    created_by UUID,
    UNIQUE (entity_id, version_num)
);

-- Enforce only one "current" version per entity
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_current_version
    ON entity_version (entity_id)
    WHERE valid_to IS NULL;
```

### Foreign Keys: Two Flavors, Pick Per Relationship

**1. Stable reference (most common) — points to the entity, always resolves to "current":**
```sql
CREATE TABLE order_item (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    product_entity_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES entity(entity_id)
);
```
Resolve current version via a join or view when reading.

**2. Pinned reference (for audit/legal/reproducibility) — points to an exact version:**
```sql
CREATE TABLE contract_snapshot (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    pricing_version_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES entity_version(version_id)
);
```
This is immutable and safe forever — the FK target never changes underneath you.

This dual-mode is the key design decision: **most references should be "pinned" or "floating" explicitly, not implicitly.**

## Helper View for "Current" Data

```sql
CREATE VIEW entity_current AS
SELECT ev.*
FROM entity_version ev
WHERE ev.valid_to IS NULL;
```

Application code and most FKs (via the `entity` table) read through this.

## Handling Deletes / Retirement

Never hard-delete. Add a status:

```sql
ALTER TABLE entity ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
    CHECK (status IN ('active', 'retired'));
```

FKs to `entity_id` stay valid forever since the identity row never disappears — only its versions change or stop being current.

## Alternative Approaches (and why I didn't lead with them)

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Single table + `valid_from`/`valid_to` (Slowly Changing Dimension, temporal table)** | Simple, native support in Postgres/SQL Server temporal tables | FK must reference natural key + timestamp (composite), messy, most DBs don't support temporal FKs well |
| **Copy-on-write whole schema (snapshot per migration)** | Clean separation of "schema version" | Expensive, hard to query across versions, doesn't scale |
| **Event sourcing (append-only event log, materialized views for current state)** | Full history, great audit trail | Big architecture shift, complex to query "current" state efficiently without projections |
| **Bitemporal tables** | Handles "as recorded" vs "as true" time | Significant complexity, rarely needed unless compliance-driven |

If your DB supports it well (Postgres 15+ doesn't natively, SQL Server 2016+ does), **system-versioned temporal tables** can replace the manual `entity_version` pattern for simple cases — but they don't solve the FK-to-specific-version problem either; they're best for audit trails, not for relationships.

## Practical Recommendations

1. **Default all FKs to point at `entity_id`** (the stable identity), not the version. This is what 90% of relationships want.
2. **Only use pinned version FKs** where you have a specific reason (contracts, invoices, compliance snapshots, ML feature reproducibility).
3. **Enforce single-current-version** with a partial unique index (shown above) — this is the row that keeps your "current state" queries fast and correct.
4. **Add a trigger** to auto-increment `version_num` and close out the previous version's `valid_to` on insert, so application code can't get this wrong.
5. **Consider whether you need full versioning at all** vs. just an audit log (`entity_history` table populated by trigger) — versioning every table adds real complexity; only version entities where "point in time" or "rollback" matters.

## Question for You

To tailor this further — are you versioning:
- (a) **individual entity data** (e.g., product prices change over time), or
- (b) **the whole schema/database structure** (e.g., migrations, schema evolution itself)?

Your phrasing ("whole schema can be versioned") suggests (b), which is a different problem — closer to migration tooling (Flyway/Liquibase) plus possibly multi-tenant schema-per-version. Let me know which you mean and I'll adjust.

## 1) Egg Carton Repurposing Idea and Instructions

**Idea: Egg Carton Seed Starter Greenhouse**

Turn an empty egg carton into a biodegradable seedling nursery that also doubles as a mini greenhouse.

**Materials:**
- Empty cardboard egg carton
- Potting soil
- Seeds
- Plastic wrap or the carton lid
- Water
- Scissors or a nail

**Steps:**
1. If the carton has a lid, cut it off and set it aside (you'll use it as a tray or cover later).
2. Poke a small drainage hole in the bottom of each egg cup using a nail or scissors.
3. Fill each cup with potting soil, leaving about a centimeter of space at the top.
4. Plant 1–2 seeds per cup at the depth recommended on the seed packet.
5. Water gently until the soil is moist but not soaked.
6. Place the carton on the removed lid or a plate to catch drips.
7. Cover loosely with plastic wrap to create a greenhouse effect, or use the lid if it fits.
8. Set in a warm, sunny spot and mist daily to keep soil damp.
9. Once seedlings sprout and outgrow the cups, transplant them directly into the garden—the cardboard breaks down in the soil.

## 2) Date of Death for William Henry Harrison

William Henry Harrison died on April 4, 1841.

## 3) Color Grouping (Warm vs. Cool)

**Warm colors:** red, yellow, orange  
**Cool/cold colors:** green, blue, purple

## 4) Haiku

Waves crash on the shore  
Salt wind brushes past my face  
Endless blue stretches

## 1) Short Story: Maya and the Bees

Maya was seven years old, and she knew exactly three things about bees: they buzzed, they made honey, and her abuela said you should never, ever swat at them.

That last rule came in handy on a Tuesday afternoon in July, when the afternoon quiet of Willow Street was broken by a sound like a tiny lawnmower having a tantrum.

Maya looked up from her chalk drawing. Next door, old Mr. Delgado's chimney was humming.

She walked to the fence and peered through the slats. A dark ribbon of bees spiraled up from the roofline, thick as a rope, pouring out from under the eaves. Mr. Delgado stood on his porch with a rolled-up newspaper, swatting wildly at the air.

"¡Ay, no, no!" he shouted. "Not the chimney! I just fixed the chimney!"

Maya knew Mr. Delgado. He gave out full-size candy bars on Halloween and let her pick the tomatoes that grew over the fence. He was not a swatter by nature, which meant he was very scared.

"Mr. Delgado!" she called. "Stop swatting! They get angry!"

He froze, newspaper in the air. "Maya? Go inside, niña, it's dangerous!"

But Maya had been paying attention in school. Last spring, a beekeeper had visited her class with a glass box of honeycomb and told them a secret: bees don't want to hurt you. They want to go home. When bees swarm, they're not attacking — they're house-hunting.

"They're looking for a new home," Maya said. "Your chimney looks like a good home."

Mr. Delgado lowered the newspaper. "And how do I tell them it is not?"

Maya thought hard. The beekeeper had said swarms rest in a cluster while scout bees search for a permanent spot. If you gave them a better house nearby, most of them would move in on their own — no poison, no smoke, no angry bees.

"I need a cardboard box," she said. "And a lemon."

"A lemon?"

"My abuela says bees hate the smell. We can make the chimney smell bad and the box smell good."

Mr. Delgado blinked at her. Then he went inside and came back with a shoebox and a lemon from his kitchen bowl. Maya squeezed the lemon over the box, rubbed the peel along its edges, and set it on the roof ledge beside the chimney, with a little honey smeared inside — because every good house needs a snack.

Then she and Mr. Delgado retreated behind the fence and waited.

For twenty minutes, nothing. The humming continued. Maya's heart thumped. What if she was wrong? What if the bees stayed forever and Mr. Delgado had to move away?

Then a single scout bee landed on the box. Then another. Then a small, brave trickle, like water finding a new path downhill.

By suppertime, the ribbon had changed direction. The bees were streaming into the shoebox instead of the chimney, and the buzzing over the roof had softened to a sleepy, contented murmur.

Mr. Delgado called a beekeeper, who came at dusk and carried the whole box away to a farm full of orange trees. "Nice work, kid," the beekeeper told Maya. "You gave them a better option instead of a fight."

That night, Mr. Delgado knocked on Maya's door with a basket of tomatoes and a full-size candy bar. "For the hero of Willow Street," he said.

Maya grinned. She taped the candy bar wrapper to her wall, right next to her chalk drawing of a bee — not swatted, not squashed, just flying home.

Lily was only seven years old, but she had always had a special connection with insects. While other kids ran screaming from bugs, Lily would crouch down and watch them for hours.

One sweltering July afternoon, she noticed something troubling next door. Mrs. Patterson, her elderly neighbor, was standing frozen on her porch, staring up at her attic vent where a dark, buzzing cloud swirled ominously.

"A bee infestation!" Mrs. Patterson cried. "I'll have to call an exterminator, but they charge so much money, and I'm afraid they'll have to tear apart my roof!"

Lily walked closer, watching the bees with fascination rather than fear. She noticed they weren't attacking anyone—they seemed disoriented, almost lost.

"Mrs. Patterson," Lily said thoughtfully, "I don't think they want to hurt anyone. I think they're just looking for a new home. My grandpa keeps bees, and he says they get like this when they're swarming."

She ran home and returned with her grandfather's old beekeeping journal and, more importantly, his phone number. Her grandfather, a retired beekeeper, arrived within the hour with a special box and protective gear.

"You did exactly right, sweetheart," he said, ruffling Lily's hair. "Bees swarming isn't dangerous if you know how to handle them. We can relocate the whole colony instead of exterminating them."

Mrs. Patterson hugged Lily tightly. "You saved my house, and you saved the bees too! You're a little hero."

## 1) Short Story: Slow and Steady Wins the Race

Milo was a grey squirrel with a shiny red bicycle and a habit of winning. Every autumn, the woodland held a race around the Great Oak, and every autumn, Milo finished first—coasting across the finish line with a flick of his tail and a grin at the crowd.

This year, a young tortoise named Tilly entered. She had no bicycle. She had no shoes. She had only four small feet and a shell that made her look, as the other squirrels whispered, "like a walking pebble."

The starting whistle blew. Milo shot off like a red arrow, tires humming over roots and stones. Within minutes he was out of sight. Tilly began walking—one foot, then another, steady as rain.

Milo, halfway around, felt so sure of victory that he stopped at a blackberry patch. "A snack won't hurt," he thought. He ate, then napped in the warm sun, dreaming of the winner's wreath. When he woke, the shadows had stretched long.

He pedaled hard, but the path was unfamiliar in the dusk. He skidded on wet leaves, took a wrong turn at the fork, and had to double back. His heart hammered.

Meanwhile Tilly kept going. She did not hurry; she did not stop. She climbed the hill, crossed the stream, and rounded the Great Oak just as the moon rose.

The crowd gasped when they saw her—dusty, unhurried, and first.

Milo arrived minutes later, breathless and beaten. He looked at Tilly, who was calmly drinking water.

"How did you do it?" he asked.

"I never stopped," she said. "You did."

And the woodland learned what Tilly already knew: the race is not always to the swift, but to the one who keeps moving.

# 1) Short Story: "The Tortoise's Garden"

In a small village, a rabbit and a tortoise decided to grow gardens for the annual harvest contest. The rabbit dug quickly, planted haphazardly, and then lounged around, confident her natural speed would let her catch up on any task in minutes.

The tortoise, meanwhile, planted one seed at a time, watered consistently every morning, and pulled weeds the moment they appeared. Each day, he made slow, steady progress.

As weeks passed, the rabbit would binge-work for a day, then abandon her garden for days at a time, telling herself she'd catch up later. Weeds took over. Plants dried out from inconsistent watering.

The tortoise never stopped his simple routine. Rain or shine, he tended his garden with patient, steady effort.

When harvest day arrived, the rabbit's garden was a chaotic mess of wilted plants and weeds. The tortoise's garden overflowed with healthy, abundant vegetables.

**Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.** Consistent, patient effort over time triumphs over bursts of speed followed by neglect.

## 2) A Story of Humans on Mars

The red dust had a way of getting into everything—into the seams of your suit, the corners of your eyes, the very marrow of your dreams. Elara had been on Mars for six years now, and she no longer dreamed of Earth. When she closed her eyes, she saw ochre plains and the ghostly blue of a distant sun.

She was a botanist by trade, a gardener by calling. Her domain was the Greenhouse—a labyrinth of transparent domes and snaking tubes just outside of New Ares, the colony's capital. Inside, the air was thick and wet and smelled of loam and chlorophyll, a stolen piece of another world. Here, she coaxed life from sterile regolith, feeding it with imported nutrients and her own stubborn hope.

Her prize was a single apple tree. It had been a splinter of a thing when she'd arrived, a fragile sapling in a hydroponic sleeve. Now, it stood three meters tall, its branches heavy with small, tart fruit. It was the only tree of its kind on the planet. The other colonists called it Elara's Folly. She called it Tuesday.

Today, however, Tuesday was in trouble.

She noticed the first leaf at dawn, during her rounds. A single leaf, high on the sunward side, had curled at the edges, its vibrant green leaching into a sickly yellow. By noon, a dozen more had followed. The tree's new growth, the delicate tips of branches that reached for the artificial sun, had begun to droop.

Elara's heart, a steady metronome for six years, stuttered. She ran her fingers over the affected leaves. They were brittle, dry. Not the crispness of thirst, but something else. A pox.

She called it in. "New Ares Control, this is Elara Vance in Greenhouse Three. I have a code yellow. Potential pathogen in the primary orchard."

The response was immediate, a voice crackling with static and concern. "Copy, Greenhouse Three. We're seeing a bio-signature anomaly on your remote sensors. We're sending a team."

She didn't wait. She donned her hazard suit, the familiar weight a comfort, and began to take samples. She swabbed the leaves, the bark, the soil. Her hands, usually so steady, trembled slightly. This wasn't just a tree. It was a symbol. It was the proof that they could not just survive here, but thrive. If Tuesday died, a little bit of everyone's hope would die with it.

The team arrived—two scientists, a med-tech, and the colony's commander, a weathered man named Elias. He stood outside the dome, his faceplate reflecting the endless red. "What's the verdict, Elara?"

"I don't know yet," she admitted, her voice tight. "It's not a nutrient deficiency. It's not a fungus we've seen before. It's... angry."

They worked for hours. The samples were analyzed in the lab. The results were baffling. The pathogen was a hybrid, a chimera of a common Earth-born bacterium and a Martian extremophile, something that should not exist. It was as if the planet itself had created a custom-made assassin for her tree.

"It's learning," Elias said, his voice low. "It's adapting. Just like we are."

That night, Elara didn't sleep. She sat in the observation lounge, staring at the dome, a faint, green glow against the blackness. She thought of Earth, of the apple orchards of her childhood, the smell of autumn and the taste of cider. She thought of the first time she'd seen a seed sprout in Martian soil, the impossible, defiant green.

She made a decision.

She went back to the greenhouse, bypassing the decontamination protocols. She opened the inner airlock and stepped inside, her suit's filters working overtime. She walked to the tree, her tree, and placed her gloved hand on its trunk. It felt warm, alive.

"I'm not going to let you die," she whispered.

She didn't have a cure. She had a hypothesis. The pathogen was a hybrid, a fusion of two worlds. Maybe the cure was, too. She went to her seed vault, a frozen library of Earth's biodiversity. She found a vial of mycorrhizal fungi, a symbiote that lived in the roots of apple trees on Earth. It was a long shot. The Martian soil was toxic to it. But she had been genetically modifying it for years, on a hunch, a side project she'd never told anyone about. She called it Project Symbiote.

She injected the modified fungi directly into the tree's root system. It was a gamble. The fungi could reject the host. It could accelerate the disease. It could do nothing at all.

For three days, nothing happened. The tree continued to shed leaves. Elias urged her to give up, to quarantine the dome and burn it all. She refused.

On the fourth day, she saw it. A tiny, almost imperceptible bud, a new leaf, uncurling on a low branch. It was a deep, healthy green.

By the end of the week, the blight had retreated. The new growth was strong. The tree was scarred, but it was alive. The colony's scientists were baffled, then elated. They wanted to study Project Symbiote, to weaponize it against future threats.

Elara just sat under the tree, a single, small apple in her hand. She polished it on her sleeve and took a bite. It was the sweetest thing she had ever tasted.

She looked out through the dome at the harsh, beautiful, terrifying world beyond. She had come here to explore, to build, to conquer. But she had learned something else. She had learned to listen. The planet wasn't just a rock. It was a partner. It was a teacher. And sometimes, if you were very lucky and very stubborn, it would let you stay.

She finished the apple, core and all, and tossed the seeds into the soil. Maybe, just maybe, they would grow.
